title: Curriculum Extensions: Bringing students closer to the text with Socratic Seminars, Mock Trials, and Lit Circles
author: Danielle Washington
summary: An 8th grade ELA teacher describes three ways she extends a great-books curriculum (Wit and Wisdom and Odell) so students go deeper into texts: Socratic Seminars, mock trials, and literature circles. She explains how each is structured, from the inner and outer seminar circles with mid-seminar goal feedback to the roles in a mock trial and the rotating jobs in a literature circle. Her central claim is that these are extensions of existing units rather than an overhaul, and that the aim is doing the curriculum better rather than doing more. She closes with practical advice: start small, build structure and routines, build in reflection, and value process over perfection. The piece is a practitioner account rather than research, but it gives concrete, usable detail on discussion-based literature instruction.
points: Socratic Seminars shift the teacher from lecturer to facilitator while students pose their own questions and cite textual evidence, with an inner/outer circle format that builds in peer feedback.
Mock trials make abstract literary themes tangible by having students analyze character motivation and ethical dilemmas from multiple perspectives in assigned roles.
Literature circles give students ownership through rotating roles and choice of text, which she ties to engagement and lifelong reading.
A first-week seminar on a relatable article doubles as a diagnostic for speaking and listening standards.
Structure matters: clear roles, rubrics, and classroom management make these extension activities work.
quotes: Socratic Seminars transform the classroom into a space for inquiry, intellectual exchange, critical thinking, and active listening. Rather than answering teacher-driven questions, students pose their own inquiries and engage in respectful dialogue about a shared text.
Students are seated in two circles: the inner and outer circle. The inner circle begins the discussion while the outer circle observes to prepare to give feedback.

The power of the mock trial lies in its ability to make abstract literary themes tangible. It’s one thing to read about justice in a novel; it’s another to argue it in court, and possibly absolve a group of middle school students from guilt!

Literature circles give students ownership of their learning. In small groups, students read and discuss a text, taking on rotating roles such as discussion director, vocabulary enricher, artist and connector.
Incorporating these strategies doesn’t require an overhaul of your curriculum. Instead, think of them as extensions–ways to deepen learning around your existing units.

The extended ELA curriculum isn’t about doing more–it’s more about doing better. By integrating strategies like Socratic Seminars, mock trials, literature circles, teachers can create learning experiences that are intellectually rigorous, emotionally resonant, and deeply human.
